content: 1. Activity Programs for Overweight or Obese Children Under 59 Months: Health workers should consider referring obese children under the age of 59 months to specialist settings for treatment. This recommendation is based on systematic reviews that address the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) framework. The search strategy used to identify relevant systematic reviews included specific queries targeting studies published between 2010 and 2015. 2. Search Strategy and Systematic Review Selection: The search strategy involved combining terms related to overweight, obesity, and children under 59 months. Systematic reviews were prioritized if they included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and provided evidence assessments. Reviews published between 2010 and 2015 were evaluated for their relevance to the PICO questions. If no direct evidence was available, indirect evidence from systematic reviews addressing either the target population or intervention was considered. 3. Systematic Reviews on Obesity Interventions: A systematic review from 2015 included 90 RCTs investigating behavioral interventions (diet, exercise, or lifestyle changes) aimed at preventing weight gain in children aged 0–18 years. These interventions were conducted in primary care settings and focused on changes in BMI (Body Mass Index). Another review from 2014 assessed motivational interviewing as a counseling approach for obesity-related outcomes in children aged 5–16 years. A 2015 review examined obesity prevention programs targeting children aged 2–18 years in high-income countries. It included both RCTs and non-RCTs, with follow-ups longer than six months. Moderate-quality evidence was reported for school-based diet-only interventions. A 2014 review focused on interventions for children aged 0–5 years from socioeconomically disadvantaged or indigenous families. This review included RCTs, non-RCTs, and quasi-experimental studies but did not provide an overall quality assessment or meta-analysis. 4. Heterogeneity in Evidence: Substantial statistical heterogeneity was reported in several meta-analyses, with variability attributed to differences in intervention types, settings, baseline characteristics of participants, and age groups. Despite this, the heterogeneity was often explainable, and evidence was not downgraded for inconsistency. 5. Dietary and Physical Activity Interventions: Dietary interventions often included nutrition counseling or education, such as using board games, leaflets, or web-based information. These interventions also promoted healthy food and water consumption instead of sugary drinks. Physical activity interventions were assessed in school-based settings, with some reviews focusing on exercise-only programs. Evidence quality varied, with some reviews reporting low-quality evidence due to heterogeneity and indirectness. 6. Key Findings on BMI and Related Outcomes: Reviews reported changes in BMI and BMI z-scores as primary outcomes. For children aged 0–5 years, only a few RCTs investigated physical activity alone. The quality of evidence for dietary and lifestyle interventions was often rated as very low to low, reflecting limitations in study design, indirectness, and variability in outcomes. 7. Guidelines and Recommendations: The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) provided guidance on weight management services for overweight or obese children and young people. These services emphasize lifestyle interventions, including diet and physical activity, tailored to the needs of the target population. 8. Limitations in Evidence: Many systematic reviews did not provide overall quality assessments or conduct meta-analyses. Some reviews included data from broader age ranges (0–18 years), which may not be directly applicable to children under 59 months. Interventions were often grouped by study setting rather than intervention type, making it challenging to extract specific insights on dietary or physical activity interventions. 9. Conclusion: While there is evidence supporting the effectiveness of behavioral interventions for managing obesity in children, the quality of evidence is often low due to heterogeneity and indirectness. Further research is needed to provide more robust and targeted recommendations for children under 59 months.
